full_judgment:
S.M. Mohsen Ali, J:- This reference has been made by a Division Bench of this Court while hearing the First Appeal No. 191 of 1973, preferred by the defendant against the judgment and decree passed by the Subordinate Judge, Fourth Court, Dacca on the 19th September, 1972, in Title suit No. 161 of 1970.

2. The questions formulated and referred to for the consideration of the Full Bench are 1. Whether in a suit instituted by the plaintiff claiming to be full owner of the house for ejectment of the defendant alleged to be his licensee, after determination and/or revocation of the license, for the purpose of jurisdiction and court-fee, valuation of the suit shall be the market value of the property?

2. Whether a suit for ejectment of licensee after revocation or termination, by the plaintiff claiming to be the full owner of the suit house falls within Cl. (v) or Cl. (xii) of section 7 of the Court-fees Act, 1870?

3. These two questions concerning court-fees and valuation appear to have arisen rather as an off-shoot, which will be evident from the facts discussed later on, in the appellate stage before the Division Bench referring these questions while hearing the aforesaid first appeal. The suit has been described in the plaint to be a "suit for ejectment and for rent due and also for compensation, valued at Rs. 11000/-. The plaintiff is a registered Company and claims to be the full owner of the building, being Holding No. 10/2, Moulvi Abul Khairat Road, within Dacca Municipality and the disputed portion is the first floor of that building, consisting of five rooms with kitchen, pantry, etc. in occupation of the defendant.

4. The relevant facts and purpose of the suit, instituted on 31.10.70 by the plaintiff-Respondent, as made out in paragraph 3 of the plaint are as follows:

"The defendant was a Director-in-Charge of the plaintiff and as such he has allowed the first floor of the said premises for his accommodation. He however, resigned from the said position on 28.8,67 which was duly accepted by the 'plaintiff but he took the privilege of 'living in the said premises. He was required to leave the house but he approached the plaintiff for letting out the premises to him and on consideration of his 'past relationship the plaintiff agreed to rent out the premises to the defendant and thereupon the defendant continues to live' in the house fixing the monthly rental at Rs. 300/- per Month according to English calendar month. In the circumstances, the defendant is a tenant of the plaintiff ejectable under the law on the grounds allowed by law," and by subsequent' amendment added by Court's order dated 16.9.71.

"And even if the defendant be not regular tenant, then also in the eye of law he is only in permissive use and occupation of the premises in question as an ejectable licensee and, therefore, under the law liable to be ejected and to pay fair compensation at Rs. 300/ per month for his use and occupation of the aforesaid premises to the plaintiff".

5. Unfortunately, the defendant did not pay any rent from the very beginning of the tenancy on one plea or the other and, as such, the plaintiff terminated the tenancy by service of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act asking him to vacate the suit premises on the expiry of the month of June, 1970, that the defendant although received the notice 314 not vacate the same. According to the plaintiff the defendant is liable for arrear of rent from September, 1967 to June, 1970, amounting to Rs. 10,200/- and compensation for the month of July, 1970 to November, 1970, being monthly rental at the rate of Rs. 300/- and at the same rate for such period as he does not vacate the suit property, he has valued his claim for-rent and compensation at Rs. 11,100/- after deducting the rent of the months of September and October, 1970.having become barred by limitation, for the purposes of jurisdiction and court-fees and has paid ad-valorem court-fees thereon, and that he is prepared to pay further court-fees if necessary. Plaintiff has prayed Rs. 11,100/- against the for ejecting for a decree for being rent and/ defendant with cost the defendant from the sum of compensation of the suit, the schedule property and for allowing compensation @ Rs.10/- per day for such period as the schedule property is not vacated.

6. The defendant's case, inter alia, is that the plaintiff has no locus standi for bring, the suit as he is not the real owner of the property, that the 'suit is bad for defect of parties as actual and lawful owner of the premises has not been made a party in the suit for ejectment, that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was never served on him. His case is a complete denial of the plaintiff's allegations that was a Director-in-Charge of the plaintiff and at of the allotment of the suit premises for his accommodation in that capacity and that of his continuing as a tenant in the suit premises at Rs. 300/- per month after his resignation. On the contrary, the defendant has put forward a claim that this property belongs to his wife Begum Farida Salauddin, by virtue of an irrevocable oral gift, dated 19.2.62, made by her father, late Mr. S.A. Subhan, C.S.P. to whom the said holding originally belonged. He has further adverted to various other facts challenging the plaintiff's case, which are not necessary for us to state. He has categorically denied that he ever used and occupied the first floor of the suit holding as tenant under the plaintiff and has contended that his wife has been peacefully holding it since her acquiring right, title and interest therein by the aforesaid gift from her father.

7. Issues as to maintainability, notice under section 106, Transfer of Property Act, relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant, whether plaintiff is entitled to a decree prayed for and for other reliefs, were framed but no issue was raised as to valuation and court-fees.

8. The learned Subordinate Judge who heard the suit found that the defendant was allowed to possess the suit premises as a director of the company or as a servant of the company, that he is not a tenant under the Co so notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is not required at all to evict the defendant. According to him, the defendant is liable to pay compensation for his occupation of the suit premises at the rate of Rs. 300/- per month. He has decreed the suit directing ejectment of the defendant from the suit premises allowing Payment of compensation of Rs. 11,000/- as claimed in the plaint. The defendant thereafter has preferred the present First Appeal.

9. It appears from the letter of reference that the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant raised three points in support of the appeal, namely, (1) that in view of the specific defence that - Begum Farida Salauddin being actual owner of the suit property and she being in actual and physical possession of the same the suit as framed in her absence is bad for defect of party and the suit as framed cannot proceed and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge erred in decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff, directing ejectment of the defendant from the suit holding, (2) 'that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in decreeing the suit for ejectment of the defendant from the suit holding although the plaintiff failed to establish that the occupation of the suit premises by the defendant was as a tenant or even as a licensee and (3) that the learned Subordinate. Judge erred in decreeing the suit for ejectment in the face of the plaintiff's disputed   title in the suit holding, and that the materials oh record which do not prove that the sale dated 27th August, 1962, was acted upon and the same does not evidence an out and out sale of the suit premises as claimed by the plaintiff. Before considering those points the referring Bench thought of the requirement of examining the question of valuation and of the Court-fees of the suit payable thereon. In the memorandum of the appeal there was a ground (No. 28) raising a question of valuation and of court-fee which is as follows :

"For that the learned Subordinate Judge should have held that the suit was not properly valued and adequately stamped inasmuch as the suit was valued at Rs. 11,100/-, being only the rent and, compensation for 37 months at the rate of Rs. 300/- per month from November, 1967 to November, 1970, vide paragraph 6 and 7 of the plaint, without making any separate valuation for eviction and without payment of any court-fees thereon and, as such, the suit should have been dismissed on this ground too."

10. The referring Bench examined the provisions of section 7 of the Court-fees Act, particularly, clauses (v) (e)it should be clause (v) as it stands now, being substituted by his Court-fees ( Bengal Amendment )Act, 1935 (Ben. Act (vii of 1935 ) and the original preceding sub-clause (a), (b) (c) and (d) omitted (xi) (cc), (xii) and noted that there has not been any amendment in India like clause (xii) which has been added in Pakistan, by the Court-fees (Amendment) Ordinance, 1962 (Ordinance No. III of 1962) which may be treated as residuary provision for the purpose of a particular class of suits which do not come within the, provision expressly provided in clauses (i) to (xi). It then proceeds to observe:

"On perusal of some important decision of different High Courts of the Sub-Continent it appears that there is some for ejectment of licensee' after revocation of the licence from the land or building or garden in suit."

One line of decision are in favour of the view that such a suit is covered by clause (v) of section 7, that is to say, the property in question is the subject-matter of the suit, and the court-fee is payable according to its market value. Of course, these decisions have been given without having a similar provision as contained in clause (xii) noted above. The reason upon which the decisions are based is that there is no scope for making distinction between an ordinary suit for ejectment based on title and a suit for ejectment based on licence for the purpose of section 7(v) of the Court-fees: Act. According to this view the language of section 7(v) being clear a suit, for ejectment being also a suit for possession, is covered by clause (v) Subject matter of such a suit cannot but be property itself. The defendant's right to remain in the abuse under the licence, cannot be a subject matter of the suit or for that matter the plaintiff's right to possess the property cannot be the subject matter Of the suit.

"The, decisions taking the other view Make distinction between an ordinary suit in ejectment razed on title and a suit based on licence for the purpose of section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act. It appears that in these decisions, opinion was for Med more on the consideration of 'hardship of the plaintiff than on proper construction of language of clause (v) of section '7".

11.  Various cases of different High Courts in India on the point have been discussed and referred to, namely, Ratilal Manilal v. Chandulal Chhotalal, (1) Mt. Barkatunnisa v. Mt. Kaniza Fatime, (2) Ramraj Tewary v. Girnaudan Bhagat, (3) Seitish Kumar v. Sm. Sailabashini, (4) Bosiram Christian v. Gomesh Chandra, (5) Gojanan Nanji v. Rajeswar Krishaji, (6) Martandrao Taivaji v. Tarabai, (7) Hafiz Mohammad Fateh Nasib v. Haji Abdur Rab, (8) Ninu Gonda Rudramoni V. Chaduvula Sri Sailam, (9) Sisir Kumar Datta V. Suril Kumar Datta, (10) Birendra Kumar V. Charu Chandra, (11) Chandi Charon Das V. Susilabala Dashi, (12) Jagadish Chand Ghoss V. Basant Kumar Bose, (13)

12. Taken chronologically, it seems that the earliest reported case is that of Ramraj Tewori V. Girnandan Bhagat, (3) (decided on 30.11.1892) This was a suit, to eject tenants at 'fixed rate on account of acts alleged to have been done by them inconsistent with the purposes for which the land was let. The annual rent was Rs. 81-5-0 and the plaintiff valued his suit for: the purposes of the court-fees at Rs. 81-5-0. It was held that the suit comes under the provision of 7(v) of the Court-fees Act, 1870 within the expression "In suits for the possession of land, house and gardens according to the value of the subject matter, the suit being undoubtedly one for" the possession of land. Their Lordships observed:

"That the subject matter here cannot be treated as the 'land itself as the landlord plaintiff,  has through its tenants proprietary possession, and was is really sought is to free the land from the possession of the tenants holding as tenants at fixed rates, that is to get rid of the tenants and their tenant right and that is a relief the value of which is easily ascertainable."

13. The next case in point of time is that of Bantam Christian v. Ganesh Chandra Das Gupta (5) in notes portion, where plaintiff .alleged that the principal defendant was a licensee whose licence was put an end to and sought for a permanent injunction against the defendant restraining him from coming upon the land after having removed him therefrom and also for ejectment and damages; He valued the suit both for purposes of court-fees and jurisdiction at Rs. 146; Rs. 100/-being" the value of ejectment and injunction and Rs. 46/- being the value of damages. Defend ant contended the value as arbitrary and too low and that the valise of the suit would be the value of land which was much more than Rs. 100/-. The learned Munsif held that the value of the subject matter of litigation was the value of the right of the licensee in the land which, according to law had no value and that even if is taken as a suitor recovery of possession the subject matter of the litigation is the possession of a licensee, which the plaintiff wanted to recover from the licensee, and such possession had little or no value. On revision against it by the difendant, High Court refused to intefere u/s. 115 and to say that the decision was wrong.

14. Mt. Barkatunnisa Begum v. Ms. Kaniza Fatema and another (1): (decided' on 28.4.1926), was a suit by the mother against her laugher and son-in-law; who were living with her, asking them to quit the house as they had set up a title to the house falsely under an alleged oral gift from the Mother and. also on account of bad behavior towards her. The defendants raised under-valuation of the suit as one of the objections. It was held:

"The suit as framed is a suit for ejectment. The prayer for determination of the plaintiff's title was only incidentally made in the plaint his not denied on behalf of the defendant that at the time they entered the house the plaintiff was the owner of the house. They set up a subsequent gift from the plaintiff. The plaintiff denies that she made gift to the defendants. If the defendant can succeed in proving the oral gift, the suit will certainly be dismissed but the, valuation of the suit is to be determined not on the plea taken in the written statement but upon the allegations as made in the plaint. The plaintiff merely prays for a decree for ejectment of the defendants. The case in my opinion, comes under 3,7, CI (v) of the Court fees 'Act and the court-fee payable is according to the  market value of subject matter of the suit. The subject matter of the suit is the right to eject the defendants and the value of the right is the value at which the defendants right to remain in the house under the license of the plaintiff may be Valued see itainraj Tewari v. Giroandan Bhagat: (2)

15.  In Ratilal Monilal v. Chandilal Chhotalal, (3) on 24.9.1946, the plaintiff sued for the possession of a house alleging the defendant to be his liensee, the trial court, on the defendant's objection about Court fee, came to the conclusion relying on 5 Pat.631 supra, that the subject-matter of the suit was not the house itself but the right to eject the defendant. The learned Single Judge, before whom the matter came of revision by the defendant, could not agree with decision of the Patna High Court. In his opinion no distinction can be made between an ordinary suit in ejectment based on tittle and suit in ejectment based on license and he referred the case to the Division Bench; which also dissented from the view expressed in 5 Pat. 631 held:

"There cannot be no possible doubt about this being a suit for possession of house within the meaning of section. 7(v); Court Fees Act, and the question then is the value that should be put up on the subject-matter on the suit since under section 7(v) it is the value of the subject matter that determines the value of the suit (page 483). "In plain English the subject matter of a suit is what the suit is about. It is not the same thing as the object of the suit. The object of the suit is the claim, in other words, possession of the house. The subject of the suit is the house. That the correct view to take is, I think; "clear also from the words in section 7(v) itself. The section says that suits for the possession of land, houses or gardens are to be valued according to the subject matter, and sub-section goes on to say that where the subject wetter, is land, the value shall be determined according to clauses (a), (b), (c) or (d) and where the subject matter is a house or garden the value shall be deemed to be the market value of the house or garden. In other words, the section contemplates the subject-matter of a suit for the possession of land as being the land and the subject matter, of a suit for the possession of a garden as being the gar den and the subject matter of a. suit for the possession of a house as being the house, and there is no suggestion to be derived from the section itself or, so far as I know from any where else that the subject matter ought to be taken to be anything else. I can imagine hard cases arising out of this provision I can imagine cases where paying the Court-fee on the value of a house might in all the circumstances be an unduly heavy price to pay in the event of the suit being lost. But we cannot do anything about that. The law seems to be as I have said, and if the law is hard it can also be amended (Page 483-484).

16. In Satish Kaiser and others v. Sm. Salabashini Devi, (1) decided on 8.3.1949, the plaintiff sued for eviction of the defendant from the house belonging to her alleging the defendant to be her licensee. She valued the suit at Rs. 100/- for the prayer of ejectment and separate valuation was made for manse profits, which was objected to by the defendant that the valuation should be the value of the subject matter of the suit as provided under section 7(v) of Court-fees Act. The trial court repelled this contention holding that the plaintiff in a suit of this description could put his own valuation on the suit which if reasonable should not be interfered with. On revision by the defendants, a Single Bench of the High Court held.

"The suit is undoubtedly one for the recovery of possession of a house and it comes under section 7(v), its valuation should therefore, be made in one of the ways provided in the aforesaid clause of section 7, Court-fees Act. The plaintiff is not entitled to his own valuation in a suit of description" (page 621)

17. The learned Judge followed the decision of Bombay High Court in AIR 194.7 Bom. 482 in preference to that of Patna and Calcutta High Courts in 5 Pat 631 and 24 C.W.N. 167 (Notes), supra. He expressed his reasons as follows:

"I hold that the subject matter of the suit is the premises sought to be recovered. In this connection I would refer to the provision of section 7(xi) (cc), Court-fees Act. There a specific provision has been made for the recovery of immovable property by landlord from his tenant including a tenant holding over after the determination of the tenancy. Now, if this provision had been there, a suit by land-lord for recovery of possession of land from tenant holding over after the tenancy had been determined would have been governed by clause (v) of section 7. The legislature thought fit to provide that such a case will not be governed by clause (v) and it made a provision in clause (xi) regarding Court-fees payable in such a case. There is no corresponding provision made by the legislature in respect of licensee whose license has been revoked. It seems therefore that the legislature intended that in the case of a license the valuation of the suit should be governed by the provision of clause (v) of section 7, Court-fees Act." (Page 622).

18. In Gajanan Nanaji & others v. Rajeshwer Krishnap and others, (2) decided on 20-7-1949, the suit was by permanent lessors for possession of shop in a market building and the plaintiffs valued their leasehold right at Rs.  180/- The defendants contended that the value for jurisdiction and for Court-fees should be the market value of the shop under section 7(v) (e), Court-fees Ad and would be at least Rs. 6000/- The trial court accepted plaintiffs valuation. On revision, a Single Bench of the Nagpur. High Court held:

"Now this suit is clearly for possession of portion, of a house. Therefore, the subject matter is, so far as the question of possession is concerned is the house it does not matter what the interest in the house consisted of because the suit is not for possession Of lease-hold rights, these are intangible and are in-capable of physical possession. The tangible physical. Object of which possession is sought is the house; therefore, subject matter of the suit, so far as possession concerned is the house. With all respects to the learned Judges, I am unable to agree with the reasoning’s.

"That apart, though this is not a very material consideration, it would be unfortunate to hold that the rights to permanent possession and occupation of a valuable house whose value might well run into lacs could be determined by Court of inferior jurisdiction by the simple expedient of the plaintiff claiming that he has been given a permanent lease for only Rs. 10/- (page 238).

19. In the case of Martandrao Tatyaji v. Tarabai (1) decided on 5-12-1951, the husband sued for declaration and possession of a portion of a house against his first wife alleging that he allowed her to reside in the upper portion of the house and that he was not in good terms with her. He has married a second wife and has got two sons and a daughter by her and wanted the entire house for his own use in exclusions of the defendant, his first wife Court-fees of Rs. 35/8/- smiles being the yearly rent of the portion in Occupation, of the defendant were paid. The trial court held that the plaintiff is to pay Court-fee on the market value of the portion in possession of the defendant according to section 7(v), Court-fees Act. On revision, a single Bench of the High Court preferred to follow the Bombay view in AIR 1947 Bombay 482 to that of Patna in ILR 5 Pat, 631, supra. It observed:

"I also do not Understand how the right of a licensee to remain in a house is to be valued. The distinction made between ordinary suit in ejectment viewed on title and suit in ejectment viewed, on licence for the purposes of section 7(v) Court-fees Act is really a distinction of Substance."

20. In Hafiz Md. Fatch Nasib v. Abdur Rub and others, (2) decided on 36.4.1953, the plaintiff filed the suit for recovery of possession of certain properties forming part a public wakf, alleged to have been transferred by the previous Mutwallis treating them as secular properties, which was illegal and unauthorised being wakf property. He valued the relief at Rs. 12,000/-, and pod court-fees on that which the defendant challenged as insufficient. The trial Court held that the market value of the properties would be Rs. 40,000/- and directed the plaintiff to pay ad valorem court-fees on that amount, against that order the plaintiff moved the High Court in revision. The Division Bench which heard the matter found that the case comes under section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act, that Valuation made on the basis of document relates to the value of the properties treating them as secular properties whereas the plaintiff was claiming this property as wakf property and not as secular property and, therefore, the principle applied by the frig Court for determining the valuation of the properties is wrong.

"No objective standard will be available for determining the market value of wakf property ......."

"The subject matter of the suit, in our opinion means the interest of the plaintiff in the land or building or garden and on the allegations made in, the plaint we have no doubt that the plaintiff was seeking the relief as a Mutwalli. As a Mutvralli his interest in the disputed property will be much narrower than the interest of a full owner. In these instances, we must hold that the intest claimed by the plaintiff as Mutwalli cannot be valued at the same figure as his interest as a full owner" (Page 102):

21. in the case of Nidagoad Rudramani and another v. Chaduvula Srisailam another, (1) decided on 3.7.1973 the plaintiff sued for ejectment of the defendanti from the suit house alleged to be let into possession as  licencee and, valued the suit under section7(xi) (cc), Court-fees Act. The trial Court decided that, the value had to be computed for purposes of Court-fees under section 7(i) and riot Under section 7(xi) (cc) of the Act and called upon the plaintiff to pay ad valeted court-fees on that basis. This was challenged on revision before the High Court relying on 15 All 63 and AIR 1927 Pat. 140, supra,

22. The Single Bench of the High Court which heard the matter rejected the argument that the suit is incapable of valuation and that it comes within the preview of schedule II, Article 16 B, Court-fee Act. It was held:

"Sub-clause (e) of clause (v) under section 7 makes provision for the recovery of possession of garden or house. So Suit for recovery of possession of a house has to be valued under that sub-clause when once it is found to come under section 7(v), Courts Act Nor am I able to appreciate the force of observation (made in AIR 192 7 Pat; 140) that the subject matter of the suit is the right of the Iicencee to remain in the home. If the basis of the suit the revocation of the licence I do not see what right the licencee has to remain in the house. He is in the position of 'a trespasser and he has no right to continue in possession of the house."

23. It agreed with the decision in AIR 1947 Bom. 487 that the suit is governed by section 7(v)(e), Court-fees Act and that the court-fees has to be paid on the Market value of the house.

24. In Chandi Charan Das v. Sushilabala Dasi, (2) decided on 3.8.1954 the suit was brought for possession of certain lands on the averment that the defendant was a licence thereof and that the licence had been revoked with a prayer for manse price, and the suit was Valued for the purpose of jurisdiction at Rs. 110/-. On an objection being raised that the Munsif Court had no jurisdiction to try the suit the learned Munsif came, to the conclusion that value of the suit was well above the pecuniary jurisdiction of his court. On appeal against it this was also affirmed by the lower appellate Court. In this case, it was agreed by both the parties that the court-fees of the plaint are payable under section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act according to the value of the subject matter and that the value of the subject Matter Calculated on that basis for the purpose of court-fees Would be well beyond the jurisdiction of the learned Munsif. The question before the Division Bench was with regard to the valuation for the purpose of jurisdiction. The Division Bench found that under section 8 of the Stilts Valuation Act, section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act has been excluded from the application of the rule that the value as determinable for the purpose of jurisdiction shall be same, the question that has to be decided is what is the subject matter of the present suit After referring to two different views on this question, one is that the property over which the suit is brought is the subject Matter of the suit and the value of the property is the value of the subject matter of the suit and that the other view is that the relief that is sought in respect of the property that is the subject matter of the suit and to the cases of the Patna High Court in ILR 5. Pat. 631 and that of Bombay High Court in AIR 1947 Bom 482 Das Gupta, J. made some interesting observations-

"I' entirely agree with Maclin, J, that in section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act the Legislature use the Words "subject matter" to trine the land where relief was sought in respect of the land, because the Legislature itself, as pointed out by the learned Judge, went on to say what should be deemed to be the value where the Subject Matter is land and again what should be deemed to be the value when the subject matter is house or garden.

With due deference to the learned Judges, I am unable to see how the fact that in the Court-fees Act, the Legislature used the words in this particular sense justifies the Conclusion that in the Civil Procedure Code, the Legislature used it in thane sense. Nor can I see that the distinction sought to be made between "subject" and "object" is anything but misleading.

It will convenient to examine some uses of the words "subject matter" as used in matter outside the courts of law. A professor of English literature is giving a lecture on the question whether Shakespeare and Bacon were identical person. What is the subject matter of the lecture? It is not right to say that Shakespeare is the subject matter nor is it right to say that Bacon is the subject matter. The proper answer certainly it; the subject Matter is the question of identity of Shakespeare and Racket. The lecture is about Shakespeare and Bacon but only the particular matter to which the lecturer Directs his attention can he called the subject matter. The fact that, the object of the lecturer may be to establish the identity or to demolish the theory of ideiitity of the two is no reason for not describing the question of identity of the two person as the subject matter of the lettered.

A club is considering the question whether members should came in dhoti. What is the subject neater of the discussion? The subject matter is not dhoti nor is the dress of the members. The subject matter is the desirability of main hers attending the club in dhoti.

It is clear from this examination that to say that subject matter of a suit is whit the suit is about is an unhelpful simplification of the problem, for the question will still have to be answered, what the suit about. Some people bring a suit on a claim of right of irrigation from a tank. Is the suit about water of the tank or is it about the land sought to be irrigated or is it merely about this right of irrigation? I think it is easy to agree that the best answer to the question is that the suit is about the right to irrigation and it is this right, not the tank, nor the land that is the subject-matter of the suit.

Consider another case, where a person brings a suit on a claim of ancient lights enjoyed by his house. The house is not the subject matter. The subject-matter is the relief the party claims on the averments of ancient lights.

I think it may be correctly said in all cases that as a suit is brought for a relief the subject matter is the relief. The fact that this relief is asked for in respect of movable or immovable properties does not make that property the subject Matter of the relief. My conclusion is that in the present case, accordingly; subject matter of the suit is not the property in respect of which the plaintiff claims relief but the relief itself. What is the relief he asks for lit is that the licensee should leave the land and structure thereon. The value of this is obviously very less ordinarily than the value of the property over which the license is said to have been given "(Pages 608-609).

25. The Division Bench held that the valuation of Rs. 100/- placed by the plaintiff on the relief he wants to obtain by getting rid of the licensee cannot be considered inadequate and set aside the orders of the Courts below.

26. In Birendra Kumar Datta v. Charu Chandra Datta and another, (1)decided on 26.11.1957, the suit was for declaration of title and recovery of possession of a niasonary one storied 'building on a plot of land measuring about six cottas, on the allegation that the defendant was a licensee and that the license had been terminated, valuing the suit at Rs. 100/-; the defendant objected that the suit being suit for declaration of tide and recovery of possession though as against a licensee on the case of the plaintiffs it should be valued according to the actual value of the subject matter of the license that is of plot of land and the structure standing thereon. The learned Munsif held that the case would come under section 7 clause (iv) (c) of the Court fees Act and no objective standard of valuation being available the valuation of the plaintiffs must be accepted.

27. On a revision by the defendant the Single Betich (Sen. J) disagreed with Satish Kumar v, Sailabasini Devi (2) and held:

"If the decision in Satish Kumar y. (i) The value of the subject matter of a suit to eject is the right of the licensee. Even viewed as a suit for recovery of possession, the possession of the licensee is the subject matter of the litigation and, as such, is of lesser value than the value of the property. This is the view to be found in cases in 24 C.W.N. 167, AIR Pat 141: 5 Pat 631. The decision in Pabirenda Nath v. Narendra Nath (1) inclines to this view though it does not decide the point. 15 All. 63 also supports the reasoning behind this view.

(ii) In a suit for possession from a licensee section 7 clause (v) of the Court-fees Act applies and since the subject matter cannot be valued precisely, the valuation put by the plaintiff must be accepted. Alternatively, if it be held to the governed by section 7(iv) (c) of the Court-fees Act, the plaintiff would be entitled to put his own valuation because no objective standard of valuation is available. This is the view to be found in Birendra Kumar v. Charu Chandra. (2)

(iii) In such a suit court-fees must he paid on the value of the property which is taken to be the subject matter. This is the view to be found in AIR 1949 Cal. 621, 64 C.W.N. 80 Manik Chand v. Sudir Kumar, AIR 1947 Bom 482, AIR 1950 Nag. 237, AIR 1952 Madhya Bharat 123 and AIR 1954 Md. 200. The decision in Kishori Mohan Ghose v. Barada Pada Chakravortti, (3) also inclines to this view.

(iv) In such a suit the subject matter of a suit is not the, property in respect of which the plaintiff claims relief but the relief itself. The relief is that the licensee should leave the land and structure thereon. The value of this obviously very less ordinarily than the value of property over which the licence was said to have been given. For the purpose of jurisdiction, the valuation need not be made on the basis of market value of the property or the capitalised value of the profit thereof. This is the view we find in the case reported in Chanel, Charon v. Susilabala. (4)

(v) The remaining point of view is that in such suit court fees must be assessed under schedule 11, Article 17, because the value is indeterminate. This is the view to be found in the cases in Manekkam Pillai v. Nagasami Aiyyar (5) and Sri Thakur Sitaramji Mandir v. Raghu Nath Das. (6)

He has also submitted that amendment that has been introduced in West Bengal after the decision of the Special Benceh case in 65 CWN 1, making definite provision for the payment of court-fees in ejecting a licensee, shows that the legislature there, in fact, has expressed its agreement with the views expressed in that case and has on appreciating the question of hardship involved in a suit for ejectment of a licensee ammended the Court-fees Act.

50. As the question of court-fee is involved, we wanted the Attorney General to appear and to express opinion on behalf of the Government. The learned Deputy Attorney General, Mt. Sultan Ahmed, has appeared on his behalf. He has more or less supported the position taken by the learned Advocate for the appellant and has argued that clause (v) of section 7 covers the case of a licensee, and hence clause (xii) is not applicable, and the court-fees are to be paid under clause (v) on the market-value of the house.

51. Mr. Fakir Abdul Mannan, the learned Advocate for the Respondent, on the other hand, has submitted that the licensee under the law does not have any possession of the subject matter, he has only some right with regard to subject matter. Section 7 clause (v) deals with land, buildings and garden when they are directly the subject-matter of the suit. He has referred to the definition of license in section 52 of the Easement Act (v of 1882) and to a decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Abdullah Bhui and others v. Ahmed Din (1) Further, he has submitted that a licensee is estopped from denying the title of his grantor under section 116 of the Evidence Act and for that matter he cannot be deemed to be treated as a trespasser in denial of his grantor's title when the license is revoked or terminated.

52. The result of the aforesaid Indian decisions and that of 65 CWN 1 (Special Bench) and AIR 1963 Pat. 308, (Full Bench) as discussed above shows that in India in a suit for ejectment of a license court-fee is to be paid according to the market value of the property from which the defendant is sought to be ejected irrespective of the right said to have been enjoyed by the licensee, as it stood before the amendment introduced in West Bengal in 1963, as a result of the Special Bench decision in 65 CWN 1 by which the licensees have been placed in a separate category by introducing cl. (V-A) and the court-fees is to be paid in case of licensee of the immovable property according to the license fees, if any, of the immovable property payable for the year next before the date of presenting plaint and where there is no license fee payable according to the amount at which the relief sought is valued. This amendment appears to be in recognition of the views in India that under the Court-fees Act the use and occupation of the licensee has been treated as possession of the land, houses and garden. The West Bangal amendment has placed the licensee in a different category and it would lend support to the view, that the amendment by which cl. (xii) as introduced in Bangladesh, would cover the case of licensee as the licensee cannot be placed under cl. 7(v) of the court-fees Act simpliciter.

53. In arriving at a proper conclusion it is very much necessary to consider what is the position of a licensee under the law. Section 52 of the Easement Act defines license in the following term:

"Where one person grants to another or to a definite number of other persons, a right to do, or continue to do, in or upon the immovable property of the grantor, something which would in the absence of such rights be unlawful, and such right does not amount to an easement or an interest in the property, the right is called a license."

54. The above definition does not speak of possession at all rather it has omitted it. It says only about "right to do" and that also a qualified one, namely, which does not amount to an easement or to an interest in the property, it is purely personal between grantor and a grantee and is merely a competence to do something under a permission, which except for this permission would be unlawful, and does not confer any right in physical property. This aspect has been clearly brought out in Abdullah Bhai and others v. Ahmed Din (1) by his Lordship Kaikaous, J. In this case, although the question of court-fees was not involved, but the question was whether the defendant was a licensee or occupying the disputed shop as a lessee on the basis of the compromise deed. In drawing the distinction between a lease and a license it was observed by his Lordship while delivering the judgment of the Supreme Court of Pakistan:

"The line of demarcation between a lease and license will sometimes be very thin though there is no doubt as to the principle applicable. A lease as will appear from section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act is immoveable property. Ownership of physical property consist of a number of rights and the owner of such property when he create a lease, transfers to the lessee a part of the rights of ownership, that is, the right of enjoyment of the property for a period, for consideration. During the continuance of the lease the right of enjoyment of the property belong to the tenant and not to the landlord. The right of ownership as well as the rights of which it is composed are rights in rem and not in personam and by the lease a right in rem is transferred to the les-see. On the other hand a 'license' as will appear from its definition in section 52 of the Easemant Act is merely a competence to do something which except for this permission would be unlawful. It does not confer any rights in physical property. There is in the case of a license only a personal agreement between the licensor and the licensee where-by the licensor agrees not to interfere with the doing of particular acts on property which is in his possession. No right in rem passes to the licensee"

55. In. Halsbury's Laws of England, third Edition, Vol. 23 it has been observed:

"A license is normally created where a per-son is granted the right to use premises with-out becoming entitled to his exclusive possession thereof, or the circumstances and conduct of the parties show that all that was intended was that the grantee should be granted a personal privilege with no interest in the land. If the agreement is merely for the use of the property in a certain way and terms while the property remains in the possession and control of the owner, the agreement will operate as a license, and even though the agreement may employ words appropriate to a lease" (Page 429)

It has been further said about the nature of license-

"A mere license does not create any estate or interest in the property to which it relates, it only makes it act lawful which without it would be unlawful". (page.430)

<u>56. Thus a licensee cannot be said to possess the land, building, or house to which he has been given certain right to do, which maybe a right to use or occupation as in the present case. By sub-sequent denial by the grantor of such permissive use or occupation on the house, he cannot be deemed to have acquired a higher right than that of a licensee by simply terming him as a trespasser. The Court will not help such a trespasser in any manner to defeat the title of rightful owner if the trespasser's right can be referred to originate from a lawful agreement. Further, section 116 of the Evidence Act says that no person, who came upon any immovable property by the license of the person in possession thereof shall be permitted to deny that such person had a title to such possession at a time when such license was given. In the Law of Evidence by Woodroffe and Ameer Ali, 10th Edition (1959) Vol. III it has been observed:</u>

<u>"The rule of tenant's estoppel prevails against one who is in possession of land under a mere license. The rule as to claiming title applied to the case of a tenant, extends also to that of person coming in by permission as a mere lodger or as a servant. There is no distinction between the case of tenant and that of common licensee. Both have been led into possession by the act of the landlord, and the licensee by asking permission admits that there to a title in the land-lord and the law under such circumstances implies a tenancy". (Page 1571-72)</u>

<u>57. The Special Bench case in 65 CWN. I could chalk out as many as five different lines of opinion on this point and has well summarised the different views already quoted by me and it is needless to discuss and repeat and to make another judicial mental exercise about the applicability or otherwise of cl. (v), s.7, Court-fees Act to the case of a licensee. It shows how contentious, ambiguous and unspecific clause (v) of section 7 is, to include such a suit. Statutes-imposing pecuniary burden which Court-fees Act surely is, are to be strictly construed. It has been stated by Maxwell in his book on Interpretation of Statutes :</u>

<u>"Statutes which impose pecuniary burden are subject to the same rule of strict construction. It is well-settled rule of law that all charges upon the subject must be imposed by clear and unambiguous language, because in some degree they operate as penalties, the subject is not to be taxed unless language of the statutes clearly imposes the obligation, and language must not be strained in order to tax a transaction which, had the Legislature thought of it, would have been convered by the appropriate words. 'In a taxing act' said Rawlatt, J, "One has to look merely at what is clearly said. There is no room for any intendment. There is no equity about a tax. There is no presumption as to a tax. Nothing is to be read in, nothing is to be implied. One can only look fairly at the language used. But this strictness of interpretation may not also always enure to the subject's benefit, for if the person sought to be taxed comes within the letter of the law, he must be taxed however great the hardship may appear to the judicial mind to be". (Page 256, 12th edition).</u>

<u>58. So any ambiguity or doubt arising out of its interpretation has to be resolved in favour of the subject. The Court will surely consider the question of hardship of parties or the supposed intention of a legislature was different if it is not clear and unambiguous. Further, as has been observed by their Lordships in the Privy Council case of Raxhappa v. Shidappa, (1)</u>

<u>"The Court-fees Act was passed not to earn a litigant with a weapon of technicality against its opponent but to secure a revenue for the benefit of the state. This is evident from the character of the Act and is brought out by section 12, which makes the decision of the first Court as to value final as between the parties and enables the Court of appeal to correct any error as to this, only where the first Court decided to the determent of the revenue."</u>

<u>59. The true mode of interpreting statutes like the Court-fees Act which has been repeatedly amended is not to consider the individual section but to take them as a whole and give effect to the legislative intent on a particular matter : 18 CWN 128. In the goods of Harriet Teviot Kerr Further in the matter of payment of court-fees it is the well established principle that allegations by the plaintiff are to be considered and not the statement by the defendant in the written statement or by the final decision of the suit on merits.</u>

<u>60. It is, therefore, not necessary, as in the present case, to consider whether the defendant totally denied that he ever possessed the suit building as licensee and that the claimed that the building belonged to his wife and she has been in possession of the same peacefully and that the alleged sale did not affect his wife's title, as the consideration of the sale deed did not pass and it was never acted upon, as has been adverted to by the referring Bench. If the defendant can succeed in proving his case, the suit may be dismissed, but the valuation of the suit is to be determined not upon the plea taken in the written statement but upon the allegations as made in the plaint. Section 7 of Court-fees Act has specifically provided f respective suits and their categories with regard to computation of Court-fees stated therein. The entire section as quoted earlier will show fist none of the categories mentioned therein specify the case of a licensee, and as it stood before the amendment made in 1962, effort has been made to stretch the section, particularly clause (v) to include the suit for ejectment of a licensee. In my considered view such a suit belongs to a specific category and is not provided for by any of the categories mentioned in section 7 and, as such, should fall within clause (xii), section 7 of the Act. The reasons for holding this view have sufficiently and elaborately discussed by his Lordship A.S. Chowdhury, J. in 19 DLR 287, which I have also elaboratedly quoted while discussing that case earlier. I would be only repeating in one form or other in stating the reasons. 1, therefore, conclude by expressing my respectful agreement with the view and the opinion expressed therein, that a suit for evicting a licensee, although in that case the suit was by limited owner, falls within clause (xii) of section 7, irrespective of the fact whether the plaintiff is a full owner or a limited owner.</u>

<u>61. I, therefore, answer question No. 1 of the reference, that the market value of the house will not determine the valuation of a suit for eviction of a licensee for the purpose of jurisdiction and court fees. Such a suit therefore, as answer to question No. 2, falls within clause (xii), section 7 of the Court-fees Act and not within clause (v), section 7 of that Act.</u>

62. It may be noted, that the present suit out of which this reference has arisen is primarily a suit for ejectment of tenant and, in the alternative, as a remote possibility; if the defendant is ultimately found liable to be ejected as an ejectable licensee under the law, he should be treated as a licensee and to be ejected as such, the plaintiff has already put in requisite court-fees as regard his claim for compensation but it appears that he has not paid court-fees with regard to his prayer for ejectment. It appears from the letter of reference that the learned Advocate for the respondent conceded that there should be separate valuation for ejectment of the defendant and necessary court-fees should have been paid. He has also submitted before us, that his client is prepared to pay the necessary court-fees for purposes of ejectment on the basis of 12 months compensation For the purposes of settling the question of payment of court-fees in the suit the appellant is directed to pay the court-fees on Tk. 3600/- on the basis of Tk. 300/- as compensation that he has claimed per month within two months from date. This full Bench reference is accordingly disposed of and the First Appeal is sent back for decision on merit.

T. M. Afzal, J. While concur-ring with the views expressed by my learned brothers and the conclusions arrived at, I would like to place on record some views of my own regarding the propriety and competence of the reference under consideration, since my learned brother Mohsen Ali, J has not expressed any opinion on the question which was argued at length before us.

64. Having perused the reference made by the-Division Bench, I confess I was a little surprised and asked myself whether there was any necessity of making the reference at all. We, therefore, at the outset asked the learned Advocates appearing in the matter to address us on the maintainability and competence of the reference itself. Mr. T. H. Khan, the learned Advocate for the appellant in the First Appeal, submitted that the referring Bench differed from the Special Bench decision of the then Dacca High Court reported in 19 D.L.R. Dacca 287 on the points under consideration; the reference had been properly made. Mr. P. A. Mannan, the learned Advocate for the respondent in the First Appeal, has, however, submitted that the referring Bench having agreed with the decision of the Special Bench and having distinguished the facts of the Special Bench case with those of the present case, there was hardly any necessity for a reference to the Full Bench. The learned Deputy Attorney General who appeared pursuant to a notice issued by the Court upon the Attorney General who, we were told, was ill submitted that the decision of the Special Bench was binding on the Division Bench and as such the reference was not at all competent.

65. Before considering the submissions made by the learned Advocates it will be helpful and pertinent to refer to the provisions regarding reference to a Full Bench as laid down in Chapter VII of the High Court Rules (Volume I) which read as follows :

“1. Whenever a Division Court shall differ from any other Division Court upon a point of law or usage having the force of law, the case be referred for decision by a Full Bench.

(2) If the question arise in an appeal from an Appellate Decree or Order, the Court refer-ring the case shall state the point or points upon which they differ from the decision of a former Division Court and shall refer the Appeal for final decision by a Full Bench.

(3) If the question arise in an Appeal from an Original Decree or Order, the questions of law shall alone be referred, and the Full Bench shall return the case with an expression of its opinion upon the points of law for final adjudication by the Division Court which referred it and in case of necessity in consequence of the absence of any or either of the referring Judges, for the ultimate decision of another Division Court.

(4) If the question arise in any matter coming before a Division Court in the exercise of its Civil Revisional Jurisdiction, the point or points shall be stated as provided in rule 2 above, and the matter shall be referred for the final decision of a Full Bench.

(5) If the question arise in any case coming before a Division Court as a Court of Criminal Appeal, Reference or Revision, the Court referring the case shall state the point or points on which they differ from the decision of a former Division LOW1 and shall refer the case to a Full Bench for such orders as to such Bench may seem fit. In making the reference the referring Judges may recommend to the Chief Justice, when they so think fit, that a Full Bench of five Judges be constituted.

(6) If a Full Bench consisting of three Judges cannot come to a majority decision, they shall refer it to the Chief Justice for constitution of a larger Bench.

(7) Every decision of Full Bench shall be treated as binding on all Division Court, and Judges sitting singly, upon the point of law or usage having the force of law determined by the Full Bench, unless it be subsequently referred by a larger Bench, specially constituted consisting of such number of Judges as in each case shall have been fixed by the Chief Justice, or unless a contrary rule be laid down by the Supreme Court.

(8) The judgment of the court in all Civil and Criminal cases heard by a Full Bench shall be typed or printed and distributed for information to all the Judges of the Court."

<u>66. The Rules quoted above lay down that whenever there is a difference of opinion between two Division Courts upon a point of law or usage having the force of law, the case shall be referred to a Full Bench. In the instant case we find no difference of opinion upon a point of law between the referring Bench an any other Division Bench nor has any difference been pointed out in the order of reference. On the contrary, the learned Judges of the referring Bench agreed with the decision of the Special Bench in the facts and circumstances of that case and tried to distinguish the facts of the present case with those of the Special Bench case. Having found that the Special Bench case did not provide the necessary guidance in the consideration of the question before it, the referring Bench went further and categorically held that the facts of the case clearly attracted 7(v)(e) of the Court Fees Act. it is, therefore, not understood as to why in the absence of any difference on any point of law with another Division Bench the referring Bench considered it necessary or appropriate to refer the matter to the Full Bench.</u>

67. Furthermore, if a reference to the Full itch was considered necessary then no categorical opinion on the point referred shall have been expressed by the referring Bench either way, as has been done by the learned Judges in the reference under consideration.

<u>68. The only reason assigned by the learned Judges for making the reference has been stated to be that "the question under consideration is of great public importance". This alone, in my opinion, cannot and ought not to be a ground for making a reference to the Full Bench and however laudable may be the purpose, Courts must function in accordance with its own Rules in order to ensure consistency and settled practice Merely because a question in the opinion of some of the Judges was of great public important could not and should not be the only reason for making a reference to a Full Bench. For that matter, it may be legitimately asked as to which matter decided by this Court is not of some public importance one way or the other. The question of public importance of a matter may be an additional factor or an attending circumstance calling for decision by a larger Bench provided the matter is otherwise covered by the Rules, but that by itself cannot be the only reason or ground for making a reference to the Full Bench. Having regard to these facts and circumstances and my discussion above. I am clearly of the opinion that the reference under consideration being not in accordance with the rules was neither necessary nor competent.</u>

<u>69. There is yet another question that calls for consideration and that is with regard to the decision of the Special Bench referred to above. In the Special Bench case the plaintiff instituted the suit as a limited owner having tenancy right for eviction of a licensee and in the instant case the plaintiff claiming to be the full owner also sought eviction of a licensee. In both the cases the defendant was sought to be evicted on the ground of his being a licensee. The learned Judges has sought to distinguish the Special Bench case with the instant case on the ground that while in the former case the plaintiff was a limited owner, in the latter case the plaintiff claimed to be a full owner. This, in my opinion, was a distinction without any difference, if at all it can be called a distinction. In both the cases the right sought to be enforced was the right to possess by evicting the defendant. It was, therefore, apparent that the principle laid down in the Special Bench case was fully applicable to the facts of the instant case. The decision of the Special Bench case, therefore, in my opinion was binding on the referring Bench and more so, when the learned Judges themselves found that the view taken by the Special Bench was correct and they agreed with the decision. If however there was any doubt in the minds of the learned Judges regarding the correctness of the view taken in the Special Bench case, it could be left to be raised and decided in the appeal. In this connection I feel it appropriate to refer to an observation of Chief Justice Cornelius in the case of Province of East Pakistan v. Serajul Huq Pal wari (1).</u>

<u>"A decision by a Bench of three judges of a High Court is, by tradition and practice, invested with the highest authority. It is in the best interest of maintenance of the standing which the High Court possesses, by virtue of the position given to it by the Constitution, and the terms of the Letters Patent under which it functions, as well as its status, in the public eye, as a source of law, that the highest respect should be paid, and should be seen to be paid, by all concerned, to every decision, pronouncements on points of law by Benches composed of three or more Judges. It would have been more pleasing to find, in the judgment under appeal, some words to indicate that the need to reconsider the conclusions reached by the Special Bench had been felt in the course of or after hearing arguments, and thereafter, a Bench of five Judges had been constituted for fuller examination of the question arising."</u>

70. It is also pertinent to note in this connection that the defendant never challenged the valuation of the suit as given by the plaintiff both for court fees and jurisdiction and no issue was either raised or framed at the trial in that regard. At the hearing of the First Appeal the defendant-appellant raised only three points as mentioned by the learned Judges in their reference which however did not include the ground on valuation and court fees. It appears from the reference that the case was heard in extenso for long 7 days and all the points raised by the appellant were allowed to be fully canvassed. Yet the referring Bench did not decide any of the points raised in the First Appeal but, took up the question of valuation of court-fees on their own and ultimately referred the matter by an elaborate order to the Full Bench. When the learned Judges came to a finding of their own on the question of valuation and court fees, the entire appeal could and ought to have been decided. It is rather unfortunate that in the process four long years have elapsed between the reference and decision by us, by which time the matter could have been finally resolved and decided by the highest court if there was any appeal. The present appeal out of which the reference arose is pending before this Court since 1972 and this reference has further prolonged the matter which is yet to be finally decided.

Reference to a Full Bench.

(1) Whenever a Division court shall differ from any other Division Court upon a point of law or usage having the force of law, the case shall be referred for decision by a Full Bench.

(2) If the question arises in an Appeal from an Appellant Decree or Order, the Court referring, the case shall state the point or points upon which they differ from the decision of a former Division Court and shall refer the Appeal for final decision by a Full Bench.

92. In this connection, it will be pertinent to notice the provisions in Chapter II of the said Rules which, inter alia, read as follows :-

1. A Division Court for the hearing of appeals from the decrees or orders of subordinate Courts shall consist of two or more Judges as the Chief Justice may think fit.

(i) Provided that it shall be competent for one Judge to hear appeals and applications and Lawazimas relating thereto in all matters specified in the subjoined, except where such appeals, applications or matters involve a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, of the Government of India Act, 1935, or any order in Council made thereunder. <u>93. Now in the instant case, we have not found nor been pointed out any difference of opinion upon a point of law between the referring Bench and any other Division Court. Thus, I do not see why in the absence of any difference on a point of law and inspire of the view taken that the Special Bench case does not provide the necessary guidance, it was considered appropriate to refer the point to the Full Bench for determination which, I say with respect, is not in harmony with the Rules.</u>

94. The learned Judges, it seems, could not agree with the interpretation of the word "subject-matter in the expression "according to the value of the subject-matter" occurring in section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act as given by A. S. Chowdhury, J. in that Special Bench decision. But the interpretation of the word "subject matter" was not the decision of the case, but was only the view of the learned Judge amongst three Judges. What was decided in that case is that the suit of a limited owner seeking to eject a licensee would be governed by section 7(xii) of the Court-fees Act for the purpose of court-fee. There A. S. Chowdhury, J held the view that the word "subject matter" occurring in section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act means the right sought to be established, the wrong to be remedied and the defence asserted in justification of the wrong and in that view of the matter his Lordship found it difficult to apply clause (v) in the case of ejecting a licensee by a limited owner and, therefore, held the residuary clause (xii) to be applicable in that case. The learned Referring Judges are of the view that this interpretation may be justified in .the facts of that case but section 7(v) is applicable in the facts of the instant case where the plaintiff being a full owner is seeking relief in the form of possession of immovable property of which he is out of possession and in such a case the "subject fatter" cannot be the right sought to be established and the defence asserted in justification of the wrong. So the facts of the two cases being different, as found by themselves, the learned Judges were perfectly entitled to their own views as to the application of section 7(v) in spite of the expression of opinion with regard to the phrase "subject-matter" by a learned Judge of the said Special Bench.

95. It is true in this reference we cannot go into the facts of the case but are to decide the points only as referred to us. 96. In the context of the aforesaid facts, the conclusion which initially found favour with us was that this reference was not perhaps appropriate and, if at all we would be merely answering an academic question. But ultimately, there was some sort of a consensus that we should answer the points raised before us. We have persuaded ourselves to examine the points referred to us for three reasons. Firstly because the answer may have some relevance for the disposal of the First Appeal itself. 97. I have already reproduced the two questions that have been framed by the learned Judges of the Division Bench for consideration. I may also add that the second question is the main question in this reference and that is, whether a suit for ejectment of a licensee after revocation or termination of the license by the plaintiff claiming to be the full owner of the suit house falls within clause (v) or clause (xii) of section 7 of the Court-fees Act, 1870. Chowdhury, J in the Special Bench case reported in 19 D.L.R. Dacca 287.

98. I would, however, like to dispose of the first point first with short observation on the assumption that clause (v) governs the suit in question. Section 7 of the Court-fees Act 1970, as it obtains now, is reproduced herein below in its entirety for facility of discussion:

"7. Computation of fees payable in certain suits: The amount of fee payable under this Act in the suits next hereinafter mentioned shall be computed as follows:

ii. for maintenance and annuities: In suits for maintenance and annuities or other sums payable periodically—according to the value of the subject-matter of the suit, and such value shall be deemed to be ten times the amount claimed to be payable for one year:

Provided that, in suits by widows for maintenance such value shall be deemed to be the amount claimed to be payable for one year.

iii. for movable property having a market value: In suits for movable property other than money, where the subject-matter has a market-value—according to such value at the date of presenting the plaint :

iv. for movable property of no market value : In suits—

(b) (Omitted by s.7(l) of the Court-fees (Bengal) Amendment) Act, 1935 (Ben. Act VII of 1935)

(c) for declaratory decree and consequential relief to obtain a declaratory decree or order, whore consequential relief is prayed,

In suits for the possession of land, buildings, or gardens—

(a) according to the value of the subject, matter, and such value shall be deemed to be fifteen  times the net profits which have arisen from the land, building or garden during the year next before the date of presenting the plaint, or if the court sees reason to think that such profits have been wrongly estimated, fifteen times such amount as the Court may assess as such profits or according to the market-value of the land, building or garden, (whichever is greater),

Explanation in this paragraph "building" includes a house, out-house, stable, privy, urinal, shed, hut, wall and other such structure, whether of masonry, bricks, wood, mud, metal Or any other material whatsoever :

vi. to enforce a right of pre-emption : In suit to enforce a right of pre-emption-according to the market-value of the land building or garden in respect of which the right is claimed:

Explanation—In this paragraph "building" has the same meaning as in paragraph v:

vi. A for partition and separate possession of a share of joint family property etc. In suits for partition and separate possession of a share of joint family property, or of a joint property, or to enforce a right to a share in any property on the ground that it is joint family property or joint property—

if the plaintiff has been excluded from possession of the property of which as clarifies to be a coparcener or co-owner, according to the market-value of the share in respect of which the suit instituted:

viii. to set aside an attachment : In suits to set aside an attachment of land or of an interest in land or revenue—according to the amount for which the land or interest was attached

viii. to set aside decrees: In suits to set aside decrees passed for ascertained amounts-according to the amounts of the decrees sought to be set aside, or where such decrees are not for any ascertained amounts, the fee payable shall be the same as paid on the plaints of the suits in which the questioned decrees were passed: Provided that, where such amount exceeds the value of land or interest, the amount of fee shall be computed as if the suit were for the possession of such land or interest:

(b) of a contract of mortgage—according to the amount agreed to be secured :

(d) of an award—according to the amount or value of the property in dispute :

xi. between landlord and tenant : In the following suits between landlord and tenant—

(a) for the delivery by a tenant of the counter-part of a lease,

(b) to enhance the rent of a tenant having a right of occupancy,

(c) for the delivery by a landlord of a lease.

(cc) for the recovery of immovable property from attendant including a tenant holding over after the determination of a tenancy,

(d) to contest a notice of ejectment,

(e) to recover the occupancy of (immovable property) from which a tenant has been illegally ejected by the landlord, and
