<u>99. Reading clause (v.) of section 7 as a whole, there remains little doubt that the word "subject-matter" occurring therein is referable only to land, buildings or gardens as the case may be and, if that be so, it is evident that the suit shall have to be valued according to the market value of the property in suit for the purpose of Court-fee where there is no net profit arising out of the land, building or garden dining the year next be-fore the date of presenting the plaint.</u>

100. In the Special Bench case referred to above his Lordship A. S. Chowdhury, J interpreted the expression "subject-matter" to mean a right sought to be established, wrong to be remedied and defence asserted in justification of the wrong and accordingly found it difficult to include a suit for ejectment of a licensee in that clause as the latter part of the clause cannot be made applicable in that can view of the "subject-matter". According to his Lordship, subject-matter is the right en joyed by the plaintiff. It is neither land nor building nor garden but a right that the plaintiff possesses over the same. It must be said, with due respect.to his Lordship, that there is an obvious error in this interpretation of the word "subject-mateer", as occurring in. clause (v), which is bereft of its context. Indeed it has been said by high authorities that statutory language is not read in isolation, but in its context.

101. The following passage occurs in Maxwell's "The Interpretation of Statutes" 12th Edition at page 76:

"The words of a statute, when there is doubt about their meaning, are to be understood in the sense in which they best harmonies with the subject of the enactment Their meaning is found not so much in a strictly grammatical or etymological propriety of language, nor even in its popular use, as in the subject, or in the occasion on which they are used, and the object to be attained."

102. Crawford in his statutory construction (1940) at page 351 stated as follows:

204. The context. The words, phrases, sections, sub-sections, provisos, saving clauses, in fact, every part of the statute, must be interpreted with reference to the context. This means that the court in construing a statute cannot isolate words or give them their abstract meaning or consider the different parts of the statute separately and independently. Every part of the statute must be considered togather, and considered as an integral part of the whole, and kept subservient to the general intent of the whole enactment. Each part or section of the statute subject to construction should be construed in connection with every other part or section, even sections which are invalid, or in conflict. Indeed all of the parts must be given effect according to the intent expressed or clearly revealed."

103. His Lordship's interpretation of the word may be perfectly valid in a different context, but when we read clause (v) as a whole and that being the only permissible manner in which a statute should be read and interpreted, it is difficult to escape the conclusion that the subject matter' there is the land, building or garden as the case may be.

104. That the word "subject-matter" in clause (v) is capable of bearing only one meaning as referred to above, but may as well mean a relief claimed in the suit in a different context and for a different purpose has been pointed out by Dasgupta J in two decisions of the Calcutta High Court.

105. In case of Chandi Charan Das v. Sushilabala Dasi (1) in a suit for recovery of possession from a licensee whose license had been revoked, question arose as to what would be the basis of valuation of the suit for the purpose of jurisdiction. It may be noted that both parties agreed that the court-fee payable on the plaint would be in accordance with the provisions of section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act. Das Gupta 3 held that for the purposes of jurisdiction, the subject matter of the suit was not the property in respect of which the plaintiffs claimed relief but the relief itself which was that the licensee should leave the land and the structures thereon. His Lordship found no reason to differ from the view of Macklin J (AIR 1947 Bombay 482) that for purposes of court-tee under clause (v) the subject-matter is the property itself but disagreed with the interpretation in so far as the valuation of such a suit for jurisdiction was concerned. His Lordship highlighted the meaning of "subject-matter" by giving some examples as follows: "In a lecture on the question whether Shakespeare and Bacon were identical person, the subject matter was neither Shakespeare nor Bacon but their identity; a club considering the question whether members should come in Dhoti, the subject matter was the desirability of the members attending the club in Dhoti; also in a suit to enforce a right of irrigation from a tank, the subject matter was neither tank nor the land to be irrigated but the right of irrigation. So also in a suit on a claim of ancient rights enjoyed by a house, the house was not the subject matter but the relief which the plaintiff claimed.

106.- The same learned Judge in the sub-sequent case of Manik Chard Mondal and another v. Sudhir Kumar Mandal and another (1) while considering whether the subject matter of the litigation was not the property but the right of the plaintiff to eject the licensee for purposes of court-fee observed as follows:-

“If the legislature has contented itself by merely saying that in suits for possession of lands; buildings or gardens the amount of fee payable shall be computed according to the value of the subject matter, there would have been much scope for the argument that the word. "subject-matter" should not be taken to be the same as the land, buildings or gardens. The Legislature itself, however, proceeded to add that such value should be deemed to be 15 times the net profits which have arisen from the land, building or garden during the year next before the date of presenting the plaint, or if the court sees reasons to think that such profits have been wrongly estimated, fifteen times such amount as the court may assess as such profits or according to the market value of the land, building or garden, whichever is lower and then if, in the opinion of the, court, such profits are not readily ascertainable, or assessable, or where there are no such profits according to the market value of the land, building or garden, It is true that in some cases of which mention has to be made of a decision of Patna High Court in Mussammat Barkatunnisa Begum v. Musammat Kaniz Fatema (2) and a decision in Ram Raj Tewari v. Giranandan Bhagat and Others (3) the view was taken that it is not the property over which the suit was brought that can be called the subject matter of the suit but the relief itself that is sought which is the subject matter of the suit. In the Patna case the decision was that the subject matter of the suit is the right to eject the defendants and the value of the right is that value at which the defendants right to remain in the house under the license of the plaintiff may be valued. This Court in Satish Kumar v. Sailabasini: Devi (4) took a different view. There also a person claimed possession from a licensee, as in the present case and Sen 3 held that the valuation should be made in one of the ways provided in clause (v) of section 7 of the Court-fees Act, and that the market-value of the land is the proper measure. The matter was considered at the Bombay High Court in Ratilal Mandal v. Chandulal Chhotalal (5) Macklin, 3, with whom Bavdekar, J. agreed, held that the market-value of the land itself was the basis on which the court-fees have to be computed -----

Though the view taken above which, as I have stated earlier, was also the view taken by Sen, J. in this court, might result in hardship in many cases, I am unable to see how, on an interpretation of the Statute according to recognised rules, it is possible to escape the co inclusion that this view is right. It is certainly possible to say that the subject-matter of suit is really the relief for which the suit is brought. It was in that view that this Court held in Chandi Charan Das v. Sushila bala Dasi (1) that the valuation for the purpose of jurisdiction should be made in such cases where a plaintiff asks for possession of the land from a licensee not on the basis of the market-value of the land but on the valuation of the relief he wants to obtain by getting rid of the licensee. As was, however, pointed out in that very case, the interpretation of the word "subject-matter" may well be different when the question of court-fee has to be considered under section 7(v) of the Court-Fees Act."

107. It appears that different High Courts of India have veered round the view that the "subject-matter" in clause (v) cannot be anything else but the property itself. Without burdening this Judgment by referring to huge cases of the Indian High Courts, I propose to refer to only one case and that is the case of Sisir Kumar Dutta and others v. Susil Kumar Dutta. (2) This was a Special Bench decision in which there was an exhaustive review of all the available decisions on the point. I shall refer again to this case when I take up the second question. But for the present purpose, one passage from that decision may be reproduced here:

"I have already observed that the subject-matter of a suit for eviction against a licensee whose license stands revoked and who thereupon becomes a trespasser is the property which is sought to be recovered. That being so, the value of the relief must be the value of the subject matter, namely, the property and that must be valued in accordance with section 7(v) of the Court-Fees Act."

108. In this connection, only one other case may be noticed. In the case of Jogdish Chandra v. Basant Kumar (1) their Lordships differed from the view taken in an earlier case of the same court. It was held in that earlier case (I.L.R 5 Patna 631AIR 1927 Patna 140) that the subject-matter of the suit is 'the right to eject the defendants and the value of that right is the value of which the defendant right to remain in the house under the license of the plaintiff may be valued. It may be noted that the same view was taken by A.S. Choudhury J. in the Special Bench Case of the Dacca High Court referred to above. But the Patna Full Bench held thus:

"With great respect, I find too difficult to accept the view. The defendant's right as licensees had already come to an end. The subject-matter of the suit was not, therefore, any right of the defendants as licensees: but the subject-matter was the entire property which was sought to be recovered."

109. I have already mentioned that in the context of the entire clause (v), the "subject-matter", of necessity, refers to the property itself i.e. land, buildings or gardens, This view, as seen above, is shared by most of the High Courts of India. Thus I am one with the observation of the learned Judges of the referring Bench that "In such a case the "subject-matter" cannot be the right sought to be established and the defence asserted in justification of the wrong. Hence my answer to the First question is that assuming clause (v) covers the suit of a plaintiff claiming to be the full owner of the house for ejectment of the defendant alleged to be his licensee after determination and/or revocation of the license, for the purposes of jurisdiction and court-fee, the valuation of the suit shall be the market value of the property in suit.

110. Now with that answer, we are squarely faced with the second question of the reference which, as stated earlier, is the main question and I better quote it again:-

"Whether a suit for ejectment of a licensee after revocation or termination by the plaintiff claiming to be the full owner of the suit house falls within clause (v) or clause (xii) i) of section 7 of the Court-fees Act, 1870?

111. Mr. T.H. Khan has submitted that such a suit falls within clause (v) of section 7 because it provides for suits for possession and once a license is revoked or terminated, the licensee becomes a trespasser and any suit to recover possession from him will clearly attract clause (v). If this view is correct, as Mr. T.H. Khan claims it is, clause (xii) will have no Manner of application. For this proposition, Mr. Khan has placed strong reliance on the Special Bench decision of the Calcutta High Court 65 C.W.N. 1, already referred to above. He has submitted that the Special Bench decision of the Dacca .High Court, 19 D.L.R. Dacca 287, not having considered the ratio of the Calcutta Special Bench Case that a licensee upon revocation or termination of his license becomes a trespasser, cannot be held to be authoritative for the view that clause (xii) will be attracted in such a suit.

112. Yet another branch of Mr. Khan's argument is that it is difficult to apply clause (xii) in such a suit because the expression "Value claimed" as it occurs therein is very vague and can mean anything including value of the property. He has submitted that it is not for the court of supply the omission; but if it does in one way as was done in the Special Bench Case of the Dacca High Court to mean "the 'value of the right sought to be enforced" no exception can legitimately be taken if another court reads "property" instead of 'fright".

113. Mr. F.A. Mannan has, one the other hand, submitted that a suit against a licensee whose license has been revoked or terminated not having been specifically provided for in any of the preceding clauses of section 7, clause (xii) is the only clause which will automatically govern such a case. He has relied on the aforesaid Special Bench case of the Dacca High Court in support of his submission and also contended that the status of the plaintiff, whether a limited owner or full owner, will not make any difference in the matter of application of clause (xii) Mr. Mannan has further submitted that clause (v) will be applicable in those suits where the relief for possession is primary and directly involved; but a suit for ejectment of a licensee not being a suit directly for recovery of possession, clause ( v) is not attracted in such a suit. He has also submitted that the Court-fees Act being a fiscal statute, the court should construe its provisions beneficially in favour of the litigant public and should incline to apply clause (xii) if there is the slightest doubt with regard to the application of clause (v) in such a suit.

114. The learned Deputy Attorney General started by submitting that it is possible to apply both clause (v) and clause (xii) to the clause of suits under consideration. When pointed out by us that the clauses are mutually exclusive, he finally opted for the view that clause (xii) would govern such a case.

115. Section 7 of the Court-fees Act has already been reproduced hereinbefore. It is clear that the section is meant to provide for computation of fees payable in certain suits clause (v) thereof provides for suits for the possession of land, buildings or gardens. After having provided for suits for possession of land, buildings or gardens generally irrespective of the mural relationship of the contestants with regard to the property-in-suit, the legislature, in subsequent clauses has manifestly referred to certain of such relationships and provided for different basis for computation of fees for recovery of possession in those suits other than as in clause (v). A wholesome principle is easily discernible in the matter of realizing fees in suits for possession. Under clause (v) in a suit for possession generally fees are to be computed according to the value of the subject-matter and such value shall be deemed to be fifteen times the net profits which have arisen from the land etc. during the year next before the institution of the suit or according to the market valise thereof. But in the subsequent clauses/ keeping in view certain from of juridical relationship between the contestants and the property in suit, the legislature has provided for different basis resulting in comparatively lesser amount of fees when a plaintiff claims possession of property of which the initial possession of the defendant is lawful but becomes unlawful on the date of the institution of the suit. For instance, it has been provided under clause (ix) that when a mortgagor sues for the recovery of the property mortgaged, he has to pay the court-fee according to the principal money expressed to e secured by the instrument of mortgage. Similarly, under clause (x) in suits for specific performance of a contract of sale, fee is to be paid according to the amount of the commiseration. Recovery of possession is often an usual prayer in such a suit which is always granted in case of success. Then again under clause (xi) in a suit between the landlord and tenant fable recovery of immovable property from a tenant, it is to be computed according to the amount of the rent of the immovable property payable for the year next before the date of presenting the plaint.

<u>116. It is evident that, in like manner, the suit of a licensor to recover possession from his licensee whose license has been revoked or terminated has not been expressly provided for in any of the clauses of section 7. It may be reasonably argued that such a suit being a suit for possession should come under the general provisions for suits for possession under clause (v). But then it has to be conceded that a suit of this nature is not expressly provided for either in clause (v) or in any, other clause. If that be so and indeed it is so, then in terms of clause (xii), a suit of this kind, of necessity, and by the sheer logic of permutation, comes to be governed by that clause.</u>

117. Let us examine to what extent the principle enunciated in the Special Bench Case of the Calcutta High Court, 65 .C.W.N. 1, can be accepted as an authority on which so much reliance has been placed by Mr. T.H. Khan.

The question before that Special Bench was:-

"What is the proper valuation of a suit for ejectment of a licensee upon revocation or termination of his license for purpose of (i) Court-fees and (ii) jurisdiction is there any difference in the matter between a case of revocation of license and a case of termination as distinguished from revocation of licence?"

Their Lordships after reviewing the catena of case-law on the point answered the questions in the following terms:

"I. Valuation of a suit for ejectment of a licensee, upon revocation or termination of his license, either for the purpose of court-fees or for the purpose of jurisdiction shall be made under the provision of section 7(v) of the Court-fees Act." 2. There is no difference in the manner of such valuation between a case of 'revocation of license and a case of termination of license as distinguished from revocation of license.

118. The retio in that decision, to quote from the judgment itself was "The answer to the question before me ought to be sought, in the first place, in what the position of a licensee is, After his license is revoked. In my opinion a licensee, whose license has been revoked, becomes a trespasser, just as a tenant, whose tenancy has been determined becomes a trespasser, unless law Makes him a statutory tenant.... If a licensee whose license stands revoked becomes a trespasser, then a suit for eviction of such a person undoubtedly would be a suit for possession of land house or garden and must be valued according to the value of the subject matter under section 7(v) of the Court fees Act.

119. In the first place, it may be pointed out that their Lordships were considering the case without there being clause (xii) in the Court-fees Act as in our case which was added in the then Pakistan by Ordinance LII of 1962. So, the premises are different. We do not know, said Abdullah J. rightly in the Special Bench Case, what view the Calcutta High Court would have taken if such a provisions was available to them. In that view of the matter, that decision is not quit; relevant for our present purpose. But Mr. T.H. Khan has submitted that even so the proposition of law as enunciated therein with regard to the status of a licensee after termination or revocation of license should be accepted as sound. If the proposition that a licensee becomes a trespasser upon revocation or termination of his license is correct then there is no question that a suit against him for possession would be governed by Clause (v) and not by clause (xii).

120. Upon an examination of the subject of license, I have found myself unable to accept the view that a licensee whose license has been revoked or terminated, becomes a trespasser for the purpose of a suit to evict such a licensee.

121. A license has been defined in section 52 of the Easements Act 1881 in the following terms:

"Where one person grants to another, or to a definite number of other persons, a right to do, or continue to do, in or upon the immovable property of the granter, something which would, in the absence of such right, be unlawful, and such right does not amount to an easement or an interest in the property, the right is called a license.

It will be seen that a license is a purely personal privilege which enables a licensee to do something in or upon the land of the licensor with his express or implied consent. It is merely a leave to do a thing enabling a licensee to do lawfully what he could not otherwise do except unlawfully. This right does not confer on the licensee an interest in immovable property or an easement appurtenant to some dominant tenement.

122. In Halsburys Laws of England Second Edition (Vol 20 page 8) (Landlord and tenant) it has been stated as uncle?:-

"A grant under which the grantee takes only the right to use the premises without exclusive possession operates as a license, and not as a lease. In deciding whether a grant amounts to a lease, or is only a licence, regard must be had to the substance of the agreement. If the effect of the instrument is to give the holder the exclusive right of occupation of the land, though subject to certain reservation, or to a restriction of the purposes for which it may be used, it is a lease; if the contract is merely for the use of the property in a certain way and on certain terms, while it remains in possession and control of the owner, it is a licence."

123. In the case of Abdullah Bhai and others v., Ahmed Din (1) (at page 172) their Lordships held thus:

"The right of ownership as well as the right of which it is composed are rights in rem and not in persona and by the lease a right in turn is transferred to the lessee. On the other hand a "licence," as will appear from its definition in section 52 of the Easement Act is merely a competence to do something which except for this permission would be unlawful. It does not confer any rights in physical property. There is in the case of a licence only a personal agreement between the licensor and the licensee whereby the licensor agrees not to interfere with the doing a particular acts on property which is in his possession. No right in rem passes to the licensee."

The underlining’s as made above are mine.

124. It may be pointed out that under section 116 of the Evidence Act "no person who came upon any immovable property by the license of the person in possession thereof shall be permitted to deny that such person had a title to such possession at the time when such license was given."

<u>125. Thus it appears that no interest in immovable property passes to neither a licensee nor the possession of the licensor cease at any point of time. When a license is revoked or terminated and the licensee yet continues to enjoy the personal privilege granted to him. I do not think that in order to stop him from further enjoyment of his privilege, it is necessary to bring an action for recovery of possession in the same way as it is required against a trespasser. Upon revocation of the license, the continuance of the licensee becomes unlawful no doubt; but for the purpose of a suit against him, having regard to the incidents of his right as a licensee, I think a decree for his ejectment is the proper and complete remedy and no further relief in the form of recovery of possession is called for nor required. There is and ought to be a distinction between, a trespasser who causes severance of physical possession of the owner and a licensee who continues unlawfully after termination of the license for the purpose of claiming relief in suits against each of them. In the case of the former, possession needs be recovered but in the case of the latter, there is no question of recovery of possession, for, by revoking the license, the licensor cannot be said to have lost his possession which was and has always been with him; what he needs is to remove an ungrateful creature from the immovable property in respect of which the latter continues to enjoy personal privileges in spite of the revocation/termination of his license. In that view of the matter also, a suit to evict an erstwhile licensee does not come under clause (v) of section 7 of the Court-fees Act.</u>

126. It may be observed that in West Bengal clause (V-A) has been incorporated by the Court-fees West Bengal (Amendment) Act 1963 (West Bengal Act 18 of 1963) in the following manner:

(V-A) In a suit for recovery of possession of immovable property from—

(a) A trespasser, where no declaration of title to the property is either prayed for or necessary for disposal of the suit—according to the amount at which the relief sought is valued in the plaint subject to the provisions of section 8C;

(b) A licensee upon revocation or termination of his license—

(i) Where a license fee is payable by the licensee in respect of the immovable property to which the suit refers, according to the amount of the license fee of the immovable property payable for the year next before the date, of presenting the plaint, or

(ii) where no such license fee is payable 5 by the licensee, according to the amount at which the relief sought is valued in the plaint subject to the provisions of section 8C.

127. It will be seen that the legislature in that Province must have considered the burden which a plaintiff seeking to eject his licensee would have to encounter in paying. court-fees pursuant to the decision of the Calcutta High Court (65 C.W.N. 1) already referred to before and accordingly brought about a change in the law to give relief to the litigants in such suits and, also, I venture to think, to make it more consistent in principle with the other provisions of section 7 of the Court-fees Act. I am of the view that the same purpose has been achieved in our country, in so far as a suit for ejecting a licensee is concerned, by adding clause (xii) to section 7.

128. At this stage, we may dispose of another contention of Mr. T. H. Khan as to on what basis the amount of fee shall be computed under clause (xii). The clause says "according to the value claimed." The value referred to therein is neither the value of the property nor that of the right to be asserted. It is the value of the relief which a plaintiff claims in a suit subject to the limitation contained in the clause itself, namely, such value shall not be less than a value which would attract a court-fee of less than fifteen rupees. This view about the basis of computation approximates with the aforesaid section (V-A) (b) (ii) of the amendment in West Bengal. I would like to recommend more explicit provisions in our own law to cater for suits against licensees with and without fees differently and against a trespasser where no declaration of title is either prayed for or necessary on the line of the amendment in West Bengal referred to above. But until such an amendment is brought about, in a suit to eject a licensee court-fee is to be paid according to the amount at which the relief sought is valued in the plaint subject to the limitation mentioned in clause (xii) itself.

<u>129. I have found in course of the fore-going discussion that a suit of the kind under consideration does not fit in clause v or in any other clause of section 7 and as such the residuary clause (xii) has, of necessity, to be taken recourse to. Even if there is a reasonable doubt as to whether clause (v) would be attracted in such a case then also on the well-established principle of beneficial construction of fiscal statutes, there will be no escape from the conclusion that clause (xii) would be attracted. For this proposition it will be sufficient to refer to a passage occurring in Maxwell's "The interpretation of Statutes" (12th Edition) at pag. 256:</u>

<u>"Statutes which impose pecuniary burdens are subject to the same rule of strict construction. It is well-settled rule of law that all charges upon the subject must be imposed by clear and unambiguous language, because in some degree they operate as penalties; the subject is not to be taxed unless the language of the statute clearly imposes the obligation, and language must not be strained in order to tax a transaction which, had the legislature thought of it would have been covered by appropriate words."</u>

130. For the reasons assigned, my conclusion is that a suit for ejectment of a licensee, after revocation or termination by the plaintiff claiming to be the full owner of the suit house falls within clause (xii) of section 7 of the Court-fees Act, 1870.
